newsitem.title: UK: Rate fears hit British markets after UK budget.
newsitem.headline: Rate fears hit British markets after UK budget.

text.p: Fears of higher British interest rates after Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget depressed prices of shares and government bonds on Thursday, while the pound remained firm.
City analysts say the budget was not tough enough to quell rampant consumer demand, raising the prospect of a credit tightening by the newly-independent Bank of England as early as next week.
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares, which had already come under pressure in after-hours trading last night, opened 58.5 points lower at 4,692.9.
On the government bond market, gilts were also sharply lower, opening down 27/32 at 113-30/32 for the key September contract on the floor of the LIFFE exchange.

Sterling had eased slightly from last night's levels when it hit a 61-month high of 2.9430 marks. But dealers on the foreign exchange markets said rate rise expectations had intensified ahead of next week's Bank of England monetary policy meeting.

In early trade the pound opened around one pfennig lower, but then started creeping higher to trade at 2.9360/70 marks on the basis that higher interest rates would make it a more attractive investment.
Speaking on BBC radio on Thursday morning, Brown said his budget represented a "considerable fiscal tightening" which had helped to bring a better balance between monetary and fiscal policy.
But analysts were by no means convinced that any pressure had been taken off the Bank of England to raise interest rates.

"The budget...leaves the task of slowing the consumer boom to the Bank of England, meaning that interest rates are likely to rise by around 100bp (basis points) over the remainder of this year," said Paribas strategists Paul Mortimer-Lee and Nick Parsons.
Official British interest rates are now standing at 6.5 percent.
One of the main planks of Brown's budget was a windfall tax on privatised utilities, a move which had been widely flagged by the Labour government which took office two months ago.
Shares in two victims of the tax, airport authority BAA and Railtrack actually rose in early trade after the impact of the new levy on them was viewed as lower than expected.
Shortly after the market opened, BAA was up 4-1/2 pence at 577 and Railtrack jumped 22 to 654.
